title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: Every non-null 6-regular graph has a $K_6$ minor.
context_text: All graphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges, and non-null means having at least one vertex. By Mader's theorem every $n$-vertex graph ($n\ge4$) with more than $4n-10$ edges has a $K_6$ minor, and this is tight even with minimum degree six (add a vertex adjacent to everything in a planar triangulation on $n-1$ vertices with minimum degree five), so average degree eight is needed in general. The authors ask what happens if the maximum degree is close to the average degree, or the minimum degree is large: they found $K_6$-minor-free graphs with minimum degree six and maximum degree at most nine, and $K_6$-minor-free graphs with minimum degree five, maximum degree seven and average degree arbitrarily close to $98/15$ (details omitted). They also state as open that every non-null graph with minimum degree at least seven has a $K_6$ minor, and recall Jørgensen's conjecture that every $6$-connected graph with no $K_6$ minor becomes planar after deleting some vertex. Their main result is that every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least six has a $K_6$ minor. The present conjecture, open as far as the authors know, asks whether $6$-regularity alone forces a $K_6$ minor; they even believe this holds for every non-null graph with minimum degree at least six and maximum degree at most eight.

title: Informal Conjecture: min degree $\geq 6$, max degree $\leq 8$ forces $K_6$ minor
statement_text: Every non-null graph with minimum degree at least six and maximum degree at most eight has a $K_6$ minor.
context_text: All graphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges, and non-null means having at least one vertex. By Mader's theorem every $n$-vertex graph ($n\ge4$) with more than $4n-10$ edges has a $K_6$ minor, and this is tight even with minimum degree six (add a vertex adjacent to everything in a planar triangulation on $n-1$ vertices with minimum degree five), so average degree eight is needed in general. The authors ask what happens if the maximum degree is close to the average degree, or the minimum degree is large: they found $K_6$-minor-free graphs with minimum degree six and maximum degree at most nine, and $K_6$-minor-free graphs with minimum degree five, maximum degree seven and average degree arbitrarily close to $98/15$ (details omitted). They also state as open that every non-null graph with minimum degree at least seven has a $K_6$ minor, and recall Jørgensen's conjecture that every $6$-connected graph with no $K_6$ minor becomes planar after deleting some vertex. Their main result is that every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least six has a $K_6$ minor. This statement is stated parenthetically right after the authors' conjecture that every non-null $6$-regular graph has a $K_6$ minor, as a stronger belief ('as far as we know') that it implies.
notes: Parenthetical aside following Conjecture 1.3; phrased as 'as far as we know'.

title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: Every non-null graph with minimum degree at least seven has a $K_6$ minor.
context_text: Both Conjecture 1.3 and Conjecture 1.4 are stated as open problems; the existence of $K_6$-minor-free graphs with minimum degree six and maximum degree at most nine shows that minimum degree six alone is not sufficient without additional degree constraints.

title: Jørgensen's Conjecture (Conjecture 1.5)
statement_text: Every 6-connected graph with no $K_6$ minor can be made planar by deleting some vertex, and therefore has a vertex of degree at most six.
context_text: Jørgensen's conjecture is introduced as a well-known related open problem. The paper's Theorem 1.7 was motivated by a step in the proof of [5] (that every graph with no $K_6$ minor is five-colourable), where Mader's theorem was used in place of 1.7 to handle bipartite substructures arising from Tutte's theorem applied to a hypothetical counterexample.
paper_contribution: The paper makes no direct progress on Jørgensen's conjecture; Theorem 1.7 is noted as related and was motivated by an approach to the five-colourability result connected to this conjecture.
notes: Attributed to Jørgensen [3]; bibliography not included in extracted text so attributed_year is null.

title: Open Question: minimum degree five in Theorem 1.6
statement_text: We do not know whether ``six'' can be replaced by ``five'' in the theorem that every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least six has a $K_6$ minor; that is, does every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least five have a $K_6$ minor?
context_text: All graphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges, and non-null means having at least one vertex. For bipartite graphs, average degree still does not help: $K_{4,n-4}$ has $4n-16$ edges and no $K_6$ minor, so no constant smaller than eight works for average degree. The authors prove that every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least six has a $K_6$ minor, via a strengthening amenable to induction: if $G$ has a bipartition $(A,B)$ with $|A|\ge|B|>0$ and every vertex of $A$ has degree at least six, then $G$ has a $K_6$ minor. They remark that minimum degree is more difficult than average degree to work with inductively. For comparison with $K_5$: every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least four has a $K_5$ minor, while for general graphs minimum degree six is needed for $K_5$ (planar graphs of minimum degree five exist).
notes: Stated in running prose without a labelled environment.

title: Informal Conjecture: average degree $\geq 5$ and max degree $\leq 6$ forces $K_5$ minor in bipartite graphs
statement_text: Perhaps average degree at least five and maximum degree at most six will guarantee a $K_5$ minor in a bipartite graph.
context_text: All graphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges, and non-null means having at least one vertex. By Wagner's theorem every graph with $n\ge3$ vertices and more than $3n-6$ edges has a $K_5$ minor, and this is tight even for almost $6$-regular planar graphs. For bipartite graphs, $K_{3,n-3}$ has $3n-9$ edges and no $K_5$ minor (it is the only such extremal graph), so average degree alone behaves as in general; but every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least four has a $K_5$ minor (a result also stated by Barát and Wood). Bounding the maximum degree alone does not give much: there are $n$-vertex bipartite graphs with average degree at least four and maximum degree at most five with no $K_5$ minor (take five disjoint copies of $K_{3,5}$, pick a degree-three vertex $v_i$ in the $i$th copy, add two new vertices adjacent to all of $v_1,\dots,v_5$, and take disjoint unions). The authors suggest that average degree at least five together with maximum degree at most six might force a $K_5$ minor in a bipartite graph, but state they have not worked this out.
notes: Phrased as 'perhaps ... but we have not worked this out'; quite tentative.
